# Why Coolant Overflows on a Cold Engine: The Pressure Cycle Mystery

Finding a trail of coolant down your driveway is an immediate red flag, but the symptoms you described—a full overflow tank while the engine runs perfectly cool—point to a specific mechanical failure rather than a runaway overheating event. On your 1991 Toyota MR2 with the 5SFE inline-four, the combination of a cold temperature gauge and room-temperature fluid in the reservoir rules out the most common suspects like a stuck thermostat or a failed water pump. If the engine were truly boiling over due to lack of circulation, you would see high heat signatures on the gauge and hot steam rising from the expansion tank immediately after driving.

The core issue here is likely a breach in the cooling system's pressure containment, allowing fluid to escape under pressure without generating significant heat. The most probable culprit is an external leak at a pressurized joint or a compromised seal that only leaks when the system expands. As the engine heats up, the coolant increases in volume and pressure, pushing against the weakest point in the loop. If that weak point is a loose hose clamp, a cracked radiator neck, or a failing gasket outside of the combustion chamber, the fluid will be forced out before it has a chance to reach boiling temperature.

Consider the physics of the expansion tank itself. In many systems like your MR2, this isn't just a storage reservoir; it acts as a safety valve and buffer. When the coolant expands during operation, the pressure sends a portion into this tank via the overflow hose. If you check the tank while the engine is still warm or just starting to cool, you are seeing the residual volume that was pushed out due to thermal expansion, not necessarily because the system lost more fluid than it holds. However, if the overflow is dripping significantly even after the car has been sitting for a while, the system might be actively losing pressure due to an internal leak into the oil gallery or an external breach that hasn't fully sealed as temperatures drop.

A critical diagnostic step you mentioned involves checking the oil cap and dipstick once the engine cools. This is essential because a blown head gasket can sometimes present deceptive symptoms if the cylinder isn't directly firing with maximum force, though usually, combustion gases entering the coolant will create immediate overheating. If the compression leak is minor or intermittent, it might not spike the temperature gauge immediately. However, look for bubbles in the overflow tank when the engine is running; that indicates combustion gas mixing with the coolant. Alternatively, if you see a milky, chocolate-milk substance on the oil dipstick or under the oil cap, you have confirmed an internal breach where coolant is leaking into the lubrication system.

Another possibility to investigate is the integrity of the radiator cap itself. These caps maintain specific pressure ratings (often 13-16 psi for older Toyotas). If the seal inside the cap is degraded, it fails to hold back the expansion pressure, forcing coolant out through the overflow hose prematurely. You can test this by pressing the valve on the cap while the system is hot; if fluid spurts out violently without the engine overheating, the cap is the weak link.

Finally, inspect the freeze plugs (core plugs) in the block. On older engines like the 5SFE, these can corrode and blow outward, creating a leak that might not be obvious until the system reaches operating pressure. A visual inspection of the lower radiator hose connection and the heater core lines is also warranted, as vibration from driving can loosen fittings over time.

If you are comfortable with your mechanical skills, draining the system to inspect for rust or debris in the oil pan will provide immediate answers. If the fluid looks clean, the issue is likely external; if it's contaminated, the head gasket is compromised.
